Learning Objectives
Recognize and manage life-threatening heat-related conditions.
Identify and manage a spectrum of less severe heat-related conditions.
Discuss risk factors and conditions that contribute to heat-related illness.
Explain strategies for the prevention of heat-related illnesses.
Review appropriate equipment and available resources to prepare for exertional heat-related
illness during training, competition, or mass events.
Background
Exertional heat illness (EHI) comprises a spectrum of heat-related conditions.1-6

Exercise-Associated Muscle Cramps
EAMC, more commonly known as heat cramps, are painful involuntary contractions of
skeletal muscle. These typically affect the limbs, particularly the legs more often than the
arms, and less frequently involve the truncal muscles, such as the abdomen and
diaphragm. The exact pathophysiology of heat cramps is unknown; however, causes of
EAMC are multifactorial. Despite the more widely recognized term heat cramps, EAMC
are not directly caused by heat. Instead, EAMC results from prolonged exercise under
certain conditions, during or after strenuous physical activity. Heat and intense exercise
contribute to other risk factors for EAMC, such as dehydration and electrolyte
imbalances.1-6,9 (Resource 1) (Resource 2)
Exercise-Associated Collapse
May occur as collapse or heat syncope
Result of orthostatic and/or vagal response of the body to heat or intense exercise
Vasodilation and decrease in vascular resistance
Cardiovascular insufficiency
Hypothalamic and autonomic dysfunction
Quick recovery if steps are taken to improve venous return and increase perfusion

Exercise-Associated Collapse
EAC may occur as heat syncope or collapse after strenuous activity. Collapse may result
from orthostatic or vagal responses to extremes of heat or exercise. This is from
physiologic adaptations of the body during exercise to improve perfusion for
oxygenation of the muscles and vital organs and to eliminate metabolic waste products.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:05 PM
AAOS | Environmental Considerations: Heat-Related Illness

3/31

During exercise, vasodilation of blood vessels and decreased vascular resistance occur.
Contraction of muscles during physical activity manually pumps blood throughout the
body and supports blood return to the heart. The response of the body to cessation of
exercise is not immediate, resulting in blood pooling, cardiovascular insufficiency, and
hypoperfusion. Autonomic dysfunction at the hypothalamus that is slow to compensate
for this physiologic change in state also may be present. Recovery from collapse or heat
syncope is quick if steps are taken to improve venous return to increase cardiac output
and maintain adequate perfusion.1-6
Exertional Heat Exhaustion
EHE exhaustion is the most common form of heat-related illness.
Occurs in a wide range of active individuals
Often made worse by dehydration
Core body temperature less than or equal to 40°C (104°F to 105°F)
Critical to cool down immediately before progresses to heat stroke

Exertional Heat Exhaustion
EHE is the most common form of heat-related illness and occurs in a wide range of active
individuals, not just elite athletes. EHE often is made worse by dehydration and other
risk factors. EHE differs from EHS only by the level of responsiveness and core body
temperature. Although no consensus exists in the literature on the exact temperature
that serves as the threshold separating EHE from EHS, a range of less than40°C to 40.5°C
and less than 104°F to 105°F is commonly used in defining EHE; however, EHE can
quickly progress to heatstroke if not recognized and managed appropriately. Patients
with EHE must be cooled down immediately to reduce core body temperature, after
which other risk factors and/or concomitant conditions, such as dehydration and
electrolyte disturbances, are addressed. The preferred method for cooling is cold water
immersion, which is the most efficient method of cooling. If an ice bath is not available,

Exertional Heat Stroke
EHS is the most severe form of heat-related illness. Many of the signs and symptoms of
EHS overlap with those of EHE. Although no consensus exists in the literature on the
exact temperature that serves as a threshold to distinguish EHS from EHE, a range of
greater or equal to 40°C to 40.5°C and greater or equal to 104°F to 105°F is commonly
used to define EHS along with evidence of mental status changes. If EHS is not
recognized quickly or managed appropriately, considerable long-term complications will
not only affect an individual’s ability to return to exercise or sports activity but also
impair everyday bodily functions. Debilitating injuries from EHS may cause permanent
damage or even fatality. 1-6, 10-16

May be related to conditions in which an individual has increased heat production through

Epidemiology and Risk Factors
Risk factors are similar for all heat-related illnesses because they occur along a spectrum
rather than in succession. Most commonly, EHI occurs in individuals who are not
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:05 PM
AAOS | Environmental Considerations: Heat-Related Illness
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000528
7/31

acclimatized to warm training environments and who may be poorly conditioned.
Although heat alone is another common risk factor, it is not the sole cause nor is it
required for heat-related illness to occur. Heat may be related to environmental factors,
such as climate, weather, seasons, geography, and exposure risks. Humidity also factors
into the perception and response of the body to heat, often creating warmer conditions
and limiting body cooling mechanisms. 1-6, 10-16
In the absence of hot environments, heat is a catabolic by-product of energy production
by muscles; therefore, metabolic factors that affect work efficiency, heat production, and
impaired cooling contribute to heat-related illness. Similarly, social factors surrounding
the circumstances for exercise or physical activity may dictate the intensity and duration
of work and heat exposure. Many factors affect perceived ambient temperature,
especially humidity and other weather conditions that affect cooling. Perceived ambient
temperature is calculated as the WBGT and can be measured using a digital device.
Humidity increases heat stress that is placed on an individual who is exercising by
decreasing their ability to dissipate heat via evaporation, which prevents the body from
cooling. Other risk factors that reduce the ability of the body to cool also may contribute
to overheating during physical activity 1-6, 10-16 (Figures 2 and 3).

Clinical Features and Diagnosis
Heat-related illness represent a spectrum of EHI. Many of the more mild and moderate
symptoms tend to overlap because heat-related illness can progress in severity along
this spectrum. As symptoms progress and heat-related illness evolves, more severe
symptoms begin to emerge. The presentation of a particular heat-related illness
depends on the presence and degree of various symptoms that define that condition.
Although these symptoms usually progress expectedly along the spectrum of EHI, a
specific heat-related condition may present independently and not necessarily follow a
predictable pattern of progressive symptoms. This may make identifying heat-related
illness and recognizing the severity of the conditions more challenging.1-6, 10-16

Management
Knowledge of the severe complications associated with EHS is essential, and patients
must be monitored for any signs or symptoms that may suggest EHS and/or impending
multi-organ failure. Recognition of the complex overlap of many heat- and exercise-
related conditions is important. For example, collapse at the conclusion of an event or
after exercising is less concerning for cardiac pathology than collapse that occurs during
physical activity; however, collapse also may result from other conditions that may occur
during intense physical activity, including hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, EHE, EHS,
pneumothorax, asthma, or cardiac arrest. Quick triage of a symptomatic individual is
critical to stratify condition severity, allowing for activation of the emergency response
system and initiation of appropriate management in a timely fashion.1-6,10-16,21-23
Recovery from EAC, commonly referred to as heat syncope, is quick, with few, if any,
long-term complications or symptoms. Simple measures can be taken to encourage
venous return to the heart to support the circulatory system and reperfuse bodily
organs, including the brain; however, not all collapse results in a transient loss of
consciousness. Because collapse results from cardiovascular insufficiency, treatment
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:05 PM
AAOS | Environmental Considerations: Heat-Related Illness
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000528
18/31

options attempt to provide quick circulatory support to restore normal cardiac output as
the body adjusts to recover from the physiologic changes it undergoes during exercise
(ie, vasodilation, tachycardia). By placing a collapsed patient in the supine position with
the legs elevated, the pooled blood can exit peripheral vessels and soft tissues to return
to the heart and brain. Cool air (fan, air conditioning, shade) and ice packs help dissipate
heat and/or cool the core body temperature. Rehydration via oral fluids will help to
restore homeostasis and support hemodynamics, such as blood pressure and pulse.1-
6,10-16,21-23
Approaches to the management of the EHI follow a similar pattern of treatment
strategies, mostly differing by the urgency, order, and extent to which treatment options
are provided. On one end of the spectrum, with EAMC, involuntary muscle contractions
are managed via rest; rehydration; replenishment of electrolytes if likely deficient;
removal of excess clothing or padding; and travel to a location at which cooling can be
encouraged via shade, airflow, air conditioning, and/or the application of ice packs or
cold, wet cloths to the affected muscles. On the opposite end of the spectrum, with EHS,
immediate cooling is the first priority, even before seeking emergency medical services
and transportation to a nearby medical facility. Other treatment options for symptoms
associated with EHS or concomitant medical conditions can be performed as cooling
occurs, during transportation, and after the patient is brought to a hospital.1-6,10-16,21-23
The most important aspects of EHS include immediate recognition of the condition,
diagnosis via a rectal thermometer, rapid management vi cold water immersion,
transportation to a hospital only after the patient has been sufficiently cooled and is
stable. Early recognition and diagnosis of EHS are paramount to preventing or managing
a potential life-threatening condition.
